note: Arbitrary: decided by someone’s will alone, with no choice for Billy. The word points back to impressment.
Junction: the joining of the ship with the fleet. Effected: brought about.
A frigate was a fast, lighter warship used for scouting and carrying messages.
Concernment: concern or importance, an old word.
Spithead is a strait of the English Channel off Portsmouth harbour, where the fleet lay. The first mutiny broke out there in April 1797.

anchor: a second and yet more serious outbreak in the fleet at the Nore
note: The Nore is a sandbank at the mouth of the Thames. In May 1797 the fleet anchored there mutinied, known as the Mutiny of the Nore.
Melville compares the mutiny to firemen refusing to work while a city is threatened by arson.
Arson: the crime of setting fires on purpose.

anchor: the three-deckers and seventy-fours moored in her own roadstead
note: A three-decker was a ship with three gun decks. A roadstead is a sheltered anchorage near shore.
Blue-jackets: sailors of the navy, named for their blue uniform coats.

anchor: ran up with huzzas the British colors with the union and cross wiped out
note: The mutineers raised a flag with the union and cross removed, leaving the plain red flag of revolt.

anchor: the enemy’s red meteor of unbridled and unbounded revolt
note: The red flag stood for revolution, as it had in France.
Grievances: real complaints, such as pay and food.
Charles Dibdin wrote popular sea songs, such as “Tom Bowling,” that were sung widely in Britain.

anchor: no mean auxiliary to the English Government
note: Auxiliary: a helper. The songs helped the government by stirring patriotism among sailors.

anchor: the patriotic devotion of the British tar
note: Tar: a sailor, from the tarred ropes and clothes he wore.
G. P. R. James was a prolific English novelist who also wrote a history of the British navy.

note: Fastidiousness: being too fussy or delicate. The historian wishes he could skip the mutiny.

anchor: national pride along with views of policy would fain shade it off
note: Fain: gladly, willingly. Pride and policy would gladly hide the mutiny.
Blazoning: announcing proudly or publicly. Aught: anything.

anchor: parleyings between Government and the ringleaders
note: Parleyings: talks to settle a dispute.

anchor: demands deemed by the authorities not only inadmissible
note: Inadmissible: not able to be accepted.

anchor: the unswerving loyalty of the marine corps
note: Marines were soldiers carried on ships. They stayed loyal and helped officers keep order.

anchor: the distempering irruption of contagious fever
note: Irruption: a sudden violent entry. Melville compares the mutiny to a fever that breaks out in a healthy body.

anchor: helped to win a coronet for Nelson at the Nile
note: Nelson’s victory over the French at the Nile in August 1798 made him a national hero.
source: Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Nelson, Horatio Nelson, Viscount”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Nelson%2C_Horatio_Nelson%2C_Viscount

anchor: the naval crown of crowns for him at Trafalgar
note: At Trafalgar in 1805 Nelson defeated the combined French and Spanish fleets and was killed in the battle.
Plenary: complete. Absolution: forgiveness of sin. The battles cleared the mutineers’ guilt.
